questionText: I simply could not summon the courage to tell her the truth.
targetSentence: I simply could not ____ to tell her the truth.
explanation: 'Get' or 'work up the nerve' both take the definite article and are followed by the infinitive. Candidates often write 'get up the nerves', where the plural means 'anxiety' rather than 'courage'.

questionText: The question caught the spokesman completely unprepared.
targetSentence: The question caught the spokesman completely ____.
explanation: 'Catch someone off guard' takes the possessive in this longer form, and the preposition is 'off', never 'out of'. The noun is uncountable here and cannot be pluralised.

questionText: I have completely lost any awareness of how much we have already spent.
targetSentence: I have completely ____ how much we have already spent.
explanation: 'Lose track of' takes no article before 'track' and requires 'of'. Learners frequently write 'lost the track of', which reads as a literal path.

questionText: The company kept the design entirely secret until the day of the launch.
targetSentence: The company ____ until the day of the launch.
explanation: 'Under wraps' is fixed in the plural with no article, and the object sits between the verb and the phrase. Candidates writing 'under wrap' or 'under the wraps' lose the mark.

questionText: The committee decided not to hold the contractor responsible after all.
targetSentence: After all, the committee decided to ____.
correctAnswer: let the contractor off the hook
explanation: 'Let someone off the hook' separates the verb and particle around the object, and 'hook' takes the definite article. The frequent error is 'let off the contractor', which misplaces the object.

questionText: Few economists were prepared to take such a risky public position.
targetSentence: Few economists were prepared to ____ so publicly.
explanation: 'Go out on a limb' requires both the particle 'out' and the indefinite article. Candidates often drop 'out', which leaves a phrase with no idiomatic meaning at all.

questionText: Criticising the chairman publicly could easily cost you your job.
targetSentence: Criticising the chairman publicly could easily ____.
correctAnswer: put your job on the line
explanation: 'Put something on the line' places the object before the preposition and needs the definite article. Learners often write 'put on the line your job', which is not possible with a short object.

questionText: She made the remark without intending it to be taken at all seriously.
targetSentence: She made the remark entirely ____.
correctAnswer: with her tongue in her cheek
explanation: Both the bare and the possessive forms are current after 'in'. The idiom takes no article before 'tongue' when the possessive is present, and 'on cheek' is never possible.

questionText: Ramon was completely unable to cope with the demands of the new post.
targetSentence: Ramon was completely ____ in the new post.
explanation: 'Out of one's depth' takes the possessive and keeps 'depth' singular. Candidates often write 'out of depth' without the determiner, or pluralise it on the model of 'the depths'.

questionText: Clara feels entirely comfortable and confident whenever she is teaching.
targetSentence: Clara is entirely ____ whenever she is teaching.
explanation: 'In one's element' takes the possessive and no article, and 'element' is always singular. The Spanish 'en su salsa' offers no formal parallel, so the phrase must be learned whole.

questionText: By nine o'clock the party had reached its liveliest point.
targetSentence: By nine o'clock the party was ____.
explanation: 'In full swing' takes no article and cannot be modified further. Candidates frequently write 'in the full swing' or 'at full swing', both of which are marked wrong.

questionText: The whole documentary was produced with almost no money at all.
targetSentence: The whole documentary was produced ____.
explanation: 'On a shoestring' takes the indefinite article and the preposition 'on'. Learners often write 'with a shoestring', importing the instrumental preposition from the lead sentence.

questionText: Fernando bought the motorbike without giving the matter any thought at all.
targetSentence: Fernando bought the motorbike ____.
explanation: 'On a whim' requires 'on' plus the indefinite article. Candidates often write 'by a whim' or 'in a whim', neither of which is idiomatic in English.

questionText: It was the junior staff who suffered most from the criticism.
targetSentence: The junior staff were ____ most of the criticism.
explanation: 'On the receiving end of' is a fixed nominal frame requiring both the definite article and 'of'. Candidates often omit 'end', which leaves a participle with no idiomatic force.

questionText: I heard unofficially that the branch is going to close in the spring.
targetSentence: I heard ____ that the branch is going to close in the spring.
explanation: Both 'through' and 'on the grapevine' are current, always with the definite article. The noun is singular and cannot be replaced by 'vine'.

questionText: It took the new arrivals a week to work out how everything functioned.
targetSentence: It took the new arrivals a week to ____.
explanation: 'Get one's bearings' is fixed in the plural with a possessive determiner. The singular 'bearing' means 'demeanour' and would make the sentence incoherent.

questionText: Ignasi dealt with the criticism calmly and without appearing at all upset.
targetSentence: Ignasi simply ____ without appearing at all upset.
correctAnswer: took the criticism in his stride
explanation: 'Take something in one's stride' places the object before the preposition and requires the possessive. The American variant uses 'strides', which is not credited here.

questionText: The lawyer still had one clever argument that nobody else knew about.
targetSentence: The lawyer still had one clever argument ____.
explanation: 'Up one's sleeve' takes the possessive and the preposition 'up', not 'in'. The singular is fixed even when several things are being concealed.

questionText: In the end the government had to accept an unpleasant necessity and raise taxes.
targetSentence: In the end the government had to ____ and raise taxes.
explanation: 'Bite the bullet' is fixed with the definite article and takes no complement. Candidates sometimes write 'bite the bullet of raising taxes', which breaks the frame the target sentence has set up.

questionText: After years of feuding, the two families finally made peace with each other.
targetSentence: After years of feuding, the two families finally ____.
explanation: 'Bury the hatchet' takes the definite article and no complement, since the reciprocal sense is built in. Candidates often add 'with each other', which is redundant and can breach the word limit.

questionText: The speech resonated strongly with a great many of those listening.
targetSentence: The speech ____ with a great many of those listening.
explanation: 'Strike a chord' takes the indefinite article and 'with' before the audience. The homophone 'cord' is the single most frequent spelling error in this idiom.

questionText: The real negotiations were conducted in private, well away from public view.
targetSentence: The real negotiations were conducted ____, well away from public view.
explanation: 'Behind the scenes' is adverbial, fixed in the plural with the definite article. The singular 'behind the scene' refers literally to stage scenery and is not idiomatic.

questionText: Ever since the incident, Pere has been out of favour with the director.
targetSentence: Ever since the incident, Pere has been ____ the director.
explanation: 'In someone's bad books' is normally possessive, but the 'of' frame is required here because the target sentence puts the person last. The noun is always plural.

questionText: Your analysis of the problem is exactly right in every respect.
targetSentence: Your analysis of the problem ____ in every respect.
correctAnswer: hits the nail on the head
explanation: The idiom is frozen: definite article before both nouns and the preposition 'on'. Candidates often write 'hits the nail in the head', a direct calque of the Spanish 'dar en el clavo'.

questionText: Marina had no idea at all what to say when they announced the award.
targetSentence: Marina was completely ____ when they announced the award.
explanation: 'At a loss for words' takes the indefinite article and 'for', not 'of'. Candidates frequently write 'in a loss' or 'at a loss of words', both of which are marked wrong.
